The best stroller footmuff is the JJ Cole Bundle Me Bunting Bag. It wins points from parents for being compatible with all strollers, as well as its adjustable design and removable hood.
You probably know to stock up on baby mittens , snowsuits , and warm hats before your little one’s first winter. But one item you might not have on your radar is a stroller footmuff.

Also called stroller buntings, footmuffs attach to your stroller to keep baby warm and dry during cold-weather walks. They look like little sleeping bags, cocooning baby in insulated, water- or wind-resistant materials for added comfort.

A stroller footmuff might not be a must-have for every parent, but they can come in handy depending on where you live — especially in colder climates where most days are plagued by freezing temps, snow, or rain. And, unlike a blanket, footmuffs aren’t easily kicked off by a wiggly passenger.

As a mom of two living in Brooklyn, New York, I relied on mine for four winters. While not exactly an essential product, I absolutely found my footmuff much easier to use and more secure than wrapping my babies in multiple blankets during walks.

“If you live in a city and are walking around with your child in a stroller, a footmuff can be really helpful, especially for babies who are not as good at regulating temperature,” says Micah Resnick , M.D., a board-certified pediatrician in Cincinnati, Ohio, with TriHealth and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board. Of course, you can still bundle up baby in layers, he notes, but a footmuff provides “a great level of convenience and ease.”

Just note that any footmuffs designed for car seats should never include a layer of fabric between baby and the car seat or harness straps, and their face should always be uncovered in the car, per the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) . Any added bulkiness is unsafe because it can impede the way the harness works. “If using a footmuff with a car seat that you put in the stroller, remember to ALWAYS remove the footmuff before putting the car seat back in the car, as the fabric behind baby is not safe to be in the car seat when operating the vehicle,” says Tina Feeley , M.D., M.P.H., a board-certified pediatrician practicing at Chestnut Hill Pediatrics in Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board .
How I Chose the Best Stroller Footmuffs

When putting together a list of the best stroller footmuffs for babies, I started by comparing feedback on stroller footmuffs from What to Expect community and staff members. Referencing their reviews and recommendations, I compiled a list of around two dozen stroller footmuffs that received praise for their quality, compatibility, and ease of use.

Next, I interviewed three pediatricians (Dr. Resnick; Gina Posner , M.D., a board-certified pediatrician practicing at MemorialCare Medical Group in Fountain Valley, California; and Dr. Feeley, for additional information about stroller footmuffs, including how to use them safely. I also referenced information from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). And since I’m a mom of two and a former parenting editor who has tested several stroller footmuffs myself, I took my own experience into consideration, too.
Based on all of this research, I narrowed down our list of the best stroller footmuffs to the top 10 that checked the following boxes:
Has anti-slip features to prevent bunching

I also awarded “bonus points” for any compelling additional features, such as extra insulation (for footmuffs for babies in very cold climates), universal compatibility, and machine-washable constructions (they tend to get pretty dirty after walks in the snow or slush).

Ready to make your winter walks warm and cozy? Below are all of the infant- and toddler-sized bunting bags What to Expect editors and parent testers highly recommend — including the very footmuff I used throughout multiple winters without any issues.

Providing optimal warmth and versatile features at a reasonable price, the JJ Cole Bundleme Bunting Bag is our overall pick for best stroller footmuff. This product has a soft inner lining to keep your child warm in the winter, plus a nylon outer layer to keep them dry when the elements strike. I also like that it has a removable hood to better control baby's temperature.

Christine Mattheis, Group VP of Content & Brand Solutions at What to Expect, used the JJ Cole Bunting Bag with daughter Rose for two winters — first when she was between 3 and 7 months old, and again between 15 and 19 months — and found it well-insulated and easy to use.

Indeed, the ease of use is a quality many parents mention. Most rave about the multiple access points — zippers on both sides and buttons on the front — make it a breeze to adjust if the weather changes during your walk. The footmuff includes three elastic straps, one at the top and two at the sides, that fit most strollers. It also comes with a removable back panel so you can ensure baby's back remains flat when strapping them in to prevent any sliding.

Another pro for parents: JJ Cole's bunting bag is machine washable. "It got super dirty every winter and we'd throw it in the wash at least a couple of times each season, especially after we had a big snow," Christine recalls.

Technically a car seat cover, this product also functions as a footmuff if you have a travel system; it comes with a roll-away flap, which makes it easier to get baby out of a car seat with minimal disturbance. Plus, there's no extra fabric between your baby and the back of the car seat, reducing slip risk.

The two layers also make this footmuff unique. You can zip the front flap to keep your little one extra warm and protected from the elements or unzip it so their face is free on a walk . Plus, it's windproof and water-resistant for any windy or wet days.

Just remember that if your baby falls asleep in the car seat — whether in the car or stroller —you should move her to a firm, safe sleep space (like a crib, bassinet or playard) and place them on their back as soon as possible, per the AAP. (And although there isn't a set amount of time on how long baby can sleep in the car seat in the car or stroller, it’s best not to let her sleep longer than necessary.) Before you get home, keep a close eye to make sure she doesn't slump into a chin-to-chest position and that their nose or mouth aren’t covered.

What to Look for in Stroller Footmuffs
To make sure you are going to get the right stroller footmuff for your family, these are some important aspects to keep in mind when shopping for a footmuff:

Material: Just like when you're shopping for a coat, the climate you live in will most likely inform what type of material to look for in a footmuff. For instance, if you live in colder climates, you might want to look for bunting that's insulated with multiple layers of protection. However, if your area doesn't get too cold, opt for a more lightweight option to prevent overheating.

Size: Most footmuffs are designed either for newborns to 6 months or 6 months to 4 years old. When in doubt, look to the sizing guide for each product to make sure it will fit your child. “Ideally, a footmuff comes up to baby’s armpits, so the face should always not be obstructed,” says Tina Feeley , M.D., M.P.H., a board-certified pediatrician practicing at Chestnut Hill Pediatrics in Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts and member of the What to Expect Medical Review Board .

Adjustability: There are a few features that can make it easier to adjust your footmuff. Some, for example, prioritize designs that include sections that you can unzip to extend the length of the bag to fit baby as she grows. A few others on our list also provide front panels that can fold down to allow more air in if it isn't too cold out or fold up to keep baby more bundled. Your footmuff may also have an adjustable harness to ensure it's secured to the stroller.

Footmuffs are perfectly safe to use as long as they're the appropriate size for your child and properly fit your stroller. If the footmuff doesn't fit the stroller or baby correctly, the fabric could potentially cover baby's mouth as a result of bunching or the footmuff moving and pose a suffocation risk. That’s why Dr. Posner recommends footmuffs with anti-slip features to ensure your little one can’t move in their harness.

It’s also important to monitor your little one for signs of overheating , adds Dr. Resnick. “If your baby feels warm to the touch, is sweating, if their skin is red and clammy, or if they are breathing fast, unzip the footmuff.”
How do I determine if a footmuff is compatible with my stroller?

The easiest way to ensure that a footmuff you’re considering works with your stroller is to buy one provided by the same brand. (For example, if you have a Nuna stroller, you’d purchase the brand’s compatible footmuff.) But that shouldn’t rule out other universal footmuffs. For these, check the product description to see if the manufacturer lists specific brands or styles it’s compatible with. Or, prioritize adjustable features that work on a variety of strollers, such as adjustable straps and zippers, a removable back panel or expandable fabrics.
